# Analysis {#sec-analysis}

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

engine=create_engine(os.environ["AUTORACK_URL"])
df=pd.read_sql("""
select ca.county_fips, ca.year, ca.affordability_salary,
    cte.routine_cognitive_share, cte.routine_manual_share,
    cte.non_routine_cognitive_share, cte.non_routine_manual_share,
    cb.poverty_rate, cb.unemployment_rate, cb.population
from county_affordability ca
join county_task_exposure cte on ca.county_fips=cte.county_fips and ca.year=cte.year
join county_baseline cb on ca.county_fips=cb.county_fips and ca.year=cb.year
""", engine)
df["log_population"]=np.log(df["population"])
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# level model: OLS with year indicators, standard errors clustered by county
reg_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share","non_routine_manual_share",
          "poverty_rate","unemployment_rate","log_population"]

reg=df.dropna(subset=reg_cols+["affordability_salary"]).copy()

X=pd.concat([reg[reg_cols],
             pd.get_dummies(reg["year"], prefix="year", drop_first=True).astype(float)], axis=1)
X=sm.add_constant(X)

model=sm.OLS(reg["affordability_salary"], X).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": reg["county_fips"]})

reg["fitted"]=model.fittedvalues
reg["resid"]=model.resid

# log respecification, same design matrix
reg["actual_log"]=np.log(reg["affordability_salary"])
model_log=sm.OLS(reg["actual_log"], X).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": reg["county_fips"]})
reg["resid_log"]=model_log.resid
```

## Panel regression

The four task group values described in @eq-group sum to one, so all four cannot enter a regression together. One serves as the reference category, and we use non routine cognitive. Each remaining coefficient reads as the change in affordability salary associated with a shift out of non routine cognitive work and into that group, holding the controls fixed. No coefficient stands alone. Every one is a comparison against the reference. The group values sit on a zero to one scale. Per percentage point figures reported later therefore divide the estimated coefficients by 100.

Normalizing the four totals by their sum, as @sec-data describes, also resolves a collinearity problem. Left unresolved, that problem would make these coefficients unusable. The unnormalized totals in @eq-weighted carry variance inflation factors between 13 and 27. All four are employment counts, so they scale together with county size. Dividing by the four group sum removes that common scale and drops the variance inflation factors to roughly 1.

Year indicators absorb conditions common to all counties within a year. These include the 2008 recession, the recovery through the 2010s, and the price movement that affordability salary does not itself deflate. Standard errors are clustered by county. Repeated observations of the same county across fifteen years are not independent draws.

## Validation before modeling

Before estimating anything we confirm the data support the methods. We check the distributions of the four task groups and of affordability salary for skew and outliers. We confirm county year coverage across the retained panel. We also check the overlap between task groups, so that no two carry effectively the same information. @fig-dists shows the distributions.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dists
#| fig-cap: "Distributions across the 12,087 county year panel. Affordability salary is right skewed with a long upper tail; the four task groups each show real cross county spread, with non routine cognitive the largest category."

share_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share",
            "non_routine_cognitive_share","non_routine_manual_share"]

titles=["Routine Cognitive","Routine Manual","Non-Routine Cognitive","Non-Routine Manual"]

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(16,3))
sns.histplot(data=df, x="affordability_salary", bins=50, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Affordability Salary ($)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("")
for i, (col, title) in enumerate(zip(share_cols, titles), start=1):
    sns.histplot(data=df, x=col, bins=50, color="#009E73", ax=axes[i])
    axes[i].set_title(title)
    axes[i].set_xlabel("")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Affordability salary is right skewed, with a skewness of 1.17. The center sits near
\$57,000, and a long tail of high purchasing power counties extends above it. That skew
is why the diagnostics below watch the extremes of the distribution.

## Specification diagnostics

A linear model assumes the association holds at a constant rate across the range of the data. It also assumes errors that scatter symmetrically and evenly around the fit. We check those assumptions with three diagnostics: residuals plotted against fitted values, a QQ plot of the residuals, and variance inflation factors. @fig-resid-analysis shows the first two and locates the failure directly. The smoothed residual line curves rather than tracking zero. The vertical spread widens with fitted values. The model underpredicts both the least and the most affordable counties while fitting the middle well. The QQ plot bends away from normal in the upper tail, which is the graphical form of a residual skew of 1.02.

```{python}
#| label: fig-resid-analysis
#| fig-cap: "Level model diagnostics. Left: residuals against fitted values with lowess smoother; the curve away from zero at both ends shows the model underpredicting the least and most affordable counties. Right: QQ plot of residuals; the bend above the line in the upper tail reflects the residual skew of 1.02."

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13,5))

sns.scatterplot(data=reg, x="fitted", y="resid", alpha=0.1, s=5, color="grey", ax=axes[0])
sns.regplot(data=reg, x="fitted", y="resid", scatter=False, lowess=True,
            line_kws={"color":"#D55E00"}, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Residuals Against Fitted Values")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Affordability Salary ($)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual ($)")

stats.probplot(reg["resid"], dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ Plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

That failure is a result rather than a discarded attempt. The level model still delivers the interpretable estimates we report. It also establishes through its own diagnostics that the data hold structure a straight line in dollars cannot represent. Binned means plots in @sec-results put the miss in dollar terms: roughly \$8,000 to \$9,000 of underprediction at each tail.

## Log respecification

Underprediction at both extremes is the signature of a multiplicative process fit on an additive scale. The drivers of affordability act proportionally, so the same shift in an input moves a high affordability county by more dollars than a low one. Logging the target converts proportional effects into the additive form a linear model assumes. We therefore refit the same specification on log affordability salary. The diagnostics respond accordingly, as @fig-log-diag shows. Residual skew falls from 1.02 to 0.09. The spread becomes close to constant across the fitted range. The QQ plot straightens through most of its range. The log linear fit is the baseline the flexible models in the next section are measured against.

```{python}
#| label: fig-log-diag
#| fig-cap: "Log model diagnostics, same layout as the level model. The smoother lies close to zero, the spread is near constant, and the QQ plot tracks the diagonal through most of its range, showing the transformation resolves most of the level model's failure."


reg["fitted_log"]=model_log.fittedvalues

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13,5))

sns.scatterplot(data=reg, x="fitted_log", y="resid_log", alpha=0.1, s=5, color="grey", ax=axes[0])
sns.regplot(data=reg, x="fitted_log", y="resid_log", scatter=False, lowess=True,
            line_kws={"color":"#009E73"}, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Residuals Against Fitted Values")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Log Affordability Salary")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual")

stats.probplot(reg["resid_log"], dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The smoothed residual line does not lie perfectly flat even after the transformation. The departures that remain are structure a single global transformation cannot absorb, most plausibly interactions among the inputs. They are what motivates the step up in model complexity.

## Variance decomposition

Affordability salary and the task groups vary both across counties and within a county over time. The two kinds of variation carry different implications. The two manual groups vary almost entirely between counties, at roughly 10 and 25 percent within on the corrected window. That is what makes the associated affordability differences durable rather than transient. Routine cognitive is the one group with genuine within county movement, near half its variance on the corrected window.

The Census occupation coding change between 2009 and 2010, described in @sec-data, inflates apparent within county variation for the routine cognitive group. This is a feature of how the source data were coded rather than a property of the counties. We therefore repeat the main estimates on a panel restricted to 2010 onward, and additionally on pre pandemic (2010 to 2019) and post pandemic (2021 to 2023) windows. Coefficient stability across these windows is reported in @sec-results, along with the between versus within exhibits that carry the persistence claim.
